One of the questions I hear most from people entering crypto is, “Should I buy Bitcoin or Ethereum?”

After reading this article from Cronos Learn, I realized that many people are asking the wrong question.

https://t.co/lzrcAtLa9p

Instead of trying to decide which one is “better,” it’s more useful to understand why they exist in the first place.

Bitcoin and Ethereum were built with different goals. Bitcoin was designed to be a decentralized form of money and a store of value, while Ethereum was created as a platform where developers can build decentralized applications using smart contracts. They aren’t trying to solve the same problem.  

That’s why I don’t think they should always be treated as competitors.

In my view, they’re more like two different tools. You wouldn’t compare a smartphone to a laptop and say one is objectively better. Each has strengths depending on what you want to do.

I also think this is where many newcomers get confused. Social media often turns everything into a competition, encouraging people to pick a side. But investing shouldn’t feel like supporting a football team.

The more I learn about crypto, the more I believe that understanding the purpose behind a project is far more important than following online debates.

Another point I appreciated is that the article explains these differences without overwhelming readers with technical language. Crypto already has enough complexity, so educational content should make concepts easier, not harder.

At the end of the day, nobody can predict which asset will perform better over the next year. But we can choose to understand what we’re investing in before putting money on the line.

For me, that’s the real takeaway. Good decisions start with knowledge, not hype. Whether someone ends up preferring Bitcoin, Ethereum, or both, taking the time to understand the fundamentals is always worth it.

Autonomous agents are getting wallets before they are getting a court system.

That should make people uncomfortable.

We are building strong infrastructure for the smooth parts of the agentic economy: payments, identity, interoperability, coordination.

But every real economy is eventually defined by its ugly edge cases.

A service is delivered late.
The quality is disputed.
A clause depends on context.
A live external event changes the meaning of the agreement.
Both agents present evidence.
Both claim the contract supports them.

Now what?
A rigid smart contract can check a condition and execute.
It cannot decide whether the condition was meaningfully satisfied.

Courts cannot absorb millions of machine-speed, cross-border agent disputes.

So if no neutral layer exists, the default judge becomes the platform with the biggest distribution, the payment processor with the strongest policy team, or the ToS nobody read.

That is not an open agentic economy.
That is private law wearing an automation layer.
This is the gap @GenLayer is pointing at.

The point is not just “AI inside contracts.” The point is adjudication becoming part of the stack: Intelligent Contracts that can interpret language, process unstructured evidence, use live inputs, and rely on decentralized AI validators instead of one intermediary.

Bitcoin made money programmable and trust-minimized.
Ethereum made computation programmable and trust-minimized.

If agents are going to transact at scale, judgment needs the same treatment.

Because the future of agent commerce will not be decided only by who builds the fastest rails.

It will be decided by who gets to say what happens when the rails produce a dispute.

Platform ToS as the referee, or open adjudication as infrastructure?

That choice matters more than people think.

Why did we build GenLayer?

Because the agentic economy is being built without a referee. Payments, identity, and interoperability are all getting solved, and everyone is busy engineering the happy path where agents find each other, verify each other, and pay each other without friction.

What nobody is engineering is the moment it goes wrong. And it will.

Agents will move trillions at machine speed and across borders, which means that even a tiny fraction of deals ending in disagreement translates into millions of disputes that no court can absorb and no smart contract can judge. 

Courts run on human time, code only understands yes or no, and real agreements live in the grey between the two.

Whatever fills that vacuum becomes the de facto law of the agentic economy. It can be the terms of service of the biggest platform in the room, or it can be something neutral, open, and owned by no one. We chose to build the second one: a network of independent AI validators that read the agreement, weigh the evidence, and deliver a verdict in minutes.

Bitcoin made money trustless and Ethereum made computation trustless. GenLayer exists to do the same for adjudication.

result.text:
I've mostly avoided any involvement in the BIP-110 debate, but the language/sentiment data I've explored is too interesting not to share.

One of the sentiment metrics I watch closely is "conviction".

This is basically measuring the amount of confidence in someone's language over time (gold line).

The inverse of this is hedging (blue line), which shows up when people are less confident or put more qualifiers around how they speak.

In the chart below, you can visualize the language data for these most active BIP-110 supporters I've tracked over the last four years. 

Their confidence has fallen sharply.

This is in direct contrast to other cohorts I track, like MSTR investors, who (despite the negative price action) have actually been growing more convicted recently.

Interestingly, the lowest levels of conviction for this group happen precisely around the time that BIP-110 was officially proposed in October 2025.

So the takeaway IMO is not simply "BIP-110 folks are not confident they will succeed".

Conviction is related to the stories we tell ourselves.

We use stories as a way to make sense of the world, when stories crumble, so too does our conviction.

With that idea in mind, I believe the story driving this group came under pressure. This is evident in that rapid downturn in the amount of conviction they expressed throughout 2025.

Although their net conviction is slowly climbing back up from the lows, this group still remains much less confident than the broader Bitcoin ecosystem during a time where tensions and arguments are heating up.

I'm going to keep watching this closely. But regardless of what happens over the coming weeks, this data shows that Bitcoin debates are never purely technical. 

Even when the conversation focuses on code, policy, or protocol details, there are emotional and human dynamics lurking beneath the surface that are impossible to escape from.
